cards.title: 3.1 General Properties of Nonmetals and the Chemistry of Carbon
body: 3.1 General Properties of Nonmetals and the Chemistry of Carbon

**Nonmetals** are defined as chemical elements that lack metallic properties, typically characterized by high ionization energy, high electronegativity, poor thermal and electrical conductivity, and the tendency to gain or share electrons in chemical reactions.

In the modern periodic table, elements are divided into metals, nonmetals, and metalloids. While metals dominate the left and center of the table, nonmetals are situated on the far right (with the exception of hydrogen). Physically, nonmetals exhibit characteristics that are nearly opposite to those of metals. Most nonmetals are gases (such as nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine) or brittle solids (such as carbon, sulfur, and phosphorus) at room temperature, with bromine being the unique liquid nonmetal. cards.title: Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
body: Among all nonmetals, Carbon is uniquely versatile. It exists in both free and combined states. In its combined form, carbon is the central element of all organic molecules, including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and fossil fuels, and is found in inorganic deposits as carbonates (like limestone, $$CaCO_3$$) and carbon oxides. Carbon exhibits the phenomenon of allotropy, meaning it can exist in two or more different physical forms in the same state. Its primary crystalline allotropes are diamond, graphite, and fullerenes. In diamond, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid, three-dimensional tetrahedral lattice, making it the hardest known natural substance and an electrical insulator. cards.problem: The bleaching action of sulfur dioxide ($$SO_2$$) is characterized as:

steps.text: Sulfur dioxide is a strong reducing agent. It bleaches colored organic pigments by reducing them to colorless compounds.
**Step 2: Determine if it is permanent or temporary**
Because the bleached colorless molecules can be slowly re-oxidized back to their colored form by oxygen in the air, the bleaching action is temporary.
The bleaching is **temporary, based on reduction** (Option **B**).

cards.title: Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
body: Carbon forms two main gaseous oxides: Carbon Monoxide ($$CO$$) and Carbon Dioxide ($$CO_2$$). Carbon Monoxide is a highly toxic, colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas. Industrially, it is prepared by passing carbon dioxide gas over red-hot charcoal at temperatures around $$1000^\\circ\\text{C}$$: $$CO_2(g) + C(s) \\rightarrow 2CO(g)$$. In the laboratory, it is prepared by dehydrating formic acid ($$HCOOH$$) with concentrated sulfuric acid: $$HCOOH(aq) \\xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} CO(g) + H_2O(l)$$. Carbon monoxide is a powerful reducing agent used extensively in metallurgy to reduce metal oxides to their elemental form, such as in the blast furnace extraction of iron. Its toxicity stems from its ability to bind to hemoglobin $$200$$ times more tightly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and causing cellular oxygen starvation.

cards.title: Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: Solid carbon dioxide, known as "dry ice," does not melt into a liquid when heated at normal atmospheric pressure. Instead, it undergoes sublimation, transforming directly from a solid to a gas, making it incredibly useful for mess-free cold storage!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily remember the properties of carbon's main allotropes, think of their structure: **Diamond** is hard and insulating because every carbon is locked in a tight 3D tetrahedral cage, whereas **Graphite** is soft and conductive because its carbons are in flat, sliding 2D sheets with free electrons.

cards.title: 3.2 Chemistry of Nitrogen, Sulphur, and Their Compounds
body: 3.2 Chemistry of Nitrogen, Sulphur, and Their Compounds

**Nonmetal Hydrides and Oxoacids** are covalent compounds of nitrogen and sulfur (such as Ammonia, Nitric Acid, Hydrogen Sulfide, and Sulfuric Acid) that serve as critical industrial chemicals for fertilizers, explosives, and metallurgy.

Nitrogen gas ($$N_2$$) makes up about $$78\%$$ of the atmosphere by volume. In its free elemental state, nitrogen exists as a diatomic molecule ($$N \equiv N$$) held together by an exceptionally strong triple covalent bond, rendering it chemically inert under standard conditions. steps.text: Since there are $$4\\text{ moles}$$ of reactant gas and $$2\\text{ moles}$$ of product gas, high pressure ($$200\\text{ atm}$$) shifts equilibrium to the right. Since the reaction is exothermic, low temperature shifts it right, but slows the rate. Thus, a moderate compromise temperature ($$500^\\circ\\text{C}$$) is used.

cards.problem: Superheated water is pumped into deep underground deposits during the Frasch process primarily to:

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand the objective of the Frasch process**
Sulfur is a solid underground. It is insoluble in water but has a relatively low melting point ($$113^\circ\\text{C}$$/$$119^\circ\\text{C}$$).
**Step 2: Understand the role of superheated water**
Water heated under pressure to $$170^\circ\\text{C}$$ melts the solid sulfur into a liquid, allowing it to be pushed up to the surface by compressed air.
The superheated water is used to **melt the sulfur** (Option **B**).

cards.title: Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
body: Chemically, nonmetals are highly electronegative, meaning their atoms have a strong affinity for electrons. In reactions with metals, they readily accept electrons to form negatively charged anions, establishing ionic bonds. In reactions with other nonmetals, they share electrons to form stable covalent bonds. Unlike metals, which form basic oxides, nonmetals typically react with oxygen to form acidic oxides (such as sulfur dioxide, $$SO_2$$, and carbon dioxide, $$CO_2$$), although some nonmetal oxides are completely neutral (such as carbon monoxide, $$CO$$, and nitric oxide, $$NO$$). Nonmetals generally do not react with dilute acids like hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.

cards.title: Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
body: Carbon Dioxide ($$CO_2$$) is a colorless, odorless gas that is approximately $$1.5$$ times denser than air. It is prepared in the laboratory by reacting calcium carbonate (marble chips) with dilute hydrochloric acid: $$CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \\rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)$$, and produced industrially by the thermal decomposition of limestone: $$CaCO_3(s) \\xrightarrow{\\text{heat}} CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$$. When dissolved in water, carbon dioxide forms weak, unstable carbonic acid ($$H_2O(l) + CO_2(g) \\rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3(aq)$$), which can form normal carbonate salts or acidic hydrogen carbonate salts. Carbon dioxide is vital for photosynthesis in plants, serves as a refrigerant in its solid state ("dry ice"), carbonates beverages, and acts as a fire extinguisher. ### 📝 Topic Challenge (Moderate to Hard)
1. Write the balanced chemical equation for the laboratory preparation of carbon monoxide from formic acid, and explain the role of sulfuric acid in this reaction.
*Answer:* The chemical equation is: $$HCOOH(aq) \\xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} CO(g) + H_2O(l)$$. Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a powerful dehydrating agent, removing a molecule of water ($$H_2O$$) from the formic acid structure, thereby facilitating its decomposition into carbon monoxide gas.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following nonmetal oxides is completely neutral to litmus paper?

steps.text: $$CO_2$$, $$SO_2$$, and $$NO_2$$ are acidic oxides because they react with water to form acids ($$H_2CO_3$$, $$H_2SO_3$$, and $$HNO_3$$/$$HNO_2$$ respectively).
Carbon monoxide ($$CO$$) is a neutral oxide and does not react with water, acids, or bases to show any pH change.
The neutral oxide is **Carbon monoxide ($$CO$$)**, option **C**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Rhombic sulfur is readily soluble in which of the following solvents?

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the chemical nature of sulfur**
Sulfur ($$S_8$$) is a nonpolar molecular solid.
**Step 2: Apply the solubility rule 'like dissolves like'**
Nonpolar sulfur is completely insoluble in polar solvents like water and ethanol. However, it dissolves easily in nonpolar organic solvents like carbon disulfide ($$CS_2$$).
